title: Kupuj czy kup?
title_en: Kupuj or kup? — the imperative rule
note:
B1 Block 7 opener — the formation rule a2_imperative deliberately withheld ('CLOSED CHUNK SET — NOT A RULE', its own note says). This unit opens it: take the 3sg present (on/ona) form — or, for a perfective verb, the 3sg FUTURE, since perfective verbs have no present tense and their future is shaped exactly like a present — drop the ending, then add -j if what's left ends in a vowel, or leave it bare if it already ends in a consonant (including a stem that already ends in j). New structure imperative_rule, registered in SEQUENCING.md + audit.py before the audit ran.

HONEST REGULAR CORE, per the spine's own instruction: four model verbs across three present classes plus one future-shaped perfective, all producing the rule's plain output with no extra alternation — grać/gra→Graj! (present_am, add -j), kupować/kupuje→Kupuj! (present_uje, stem already ends in j), pić/pije→Pij! (present_e_esz, stem already ends in j), mówić/mówi→Mów! (present_e_isz, bare consonant stem), kupić/kupi (b1_perf_future)→Kup! (bare consonant stem, from the FUTURE not the present). FENCED, explicitly, per the spine naming this exact case: robić→rób. robić is present_e_isz just like mówić, but its imperative needs an extra o→ó vowel shift the plain rule doesn't predict — never shown, never a distractor, not even mentioned by name beyond this note. No other stem-alternating irregular appears anywhere in the pack.

RETROACTIVE PAYOFF, the actual point of the unit: four of a2_imperative's five chunk forms (czekaj, słuchaj, idź, chodź) are shown again on the first slide and named as regular instances of the SAME rule Dad is now learning — czekać→czeka→czekaj and słuchać→słucha→słuchaj are exact matches (present_am, add -j, identical mechanism to grać→graj; czeka/słucha are themselves new teaches_lemmas here, since a2_imperative's own note confirms it never showed the present-tense forms behind its five chunks, only the imperatives); iść→idzie→idź and chodzić→chodzi→chodź both carry the dzie→dź / dzi→dź softening already memorized as whole forms in A2 and are named here as 'the rule, plus one sound change you already know by heart' rather than re-derived from scratch — no new softening rule is taught, they are presented as confirmation, not exercise material. daj is DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT of this derivation: a2_imperative's own note states outright that dać is 'not in POOL, is not taught, and is never shown' — check_new.py confirmed dać and da both still NEW before this pack shipped, so daj stays exactly as opaque as A2 left it; the first slide names this explicitly rather than silently dropping the fifth word.

NEGATIVE IMPERATIVE — the aspect flip, per the spine's instruction, stated as one line and demonstrated with TWO already-owned aspect-twin pairs rather than asserted abstractly: kupić/kupować (Kup wodę! — one bottle, done, perfective — vs Nie kupuj wody! — general prohibition, must be imperfective, never Nie kup) and wypić/pić (Wypij herbatę! vs Nie pij herbaty!). Both pairs ride structures already fully owned (b1_perf_future for kupię/kupisz/kupi and wypiję/wypijesz/wypije; present_uje/present_e_esz for kupuje/pije) — nothing new is taught by the flip itself, only the naming of a fact the learner has, without realising it, already been living inside (every imperative in a2_imperative and every one of this unit's own positive models is imperfective). Genitive-under-negation on wody/herbaty rides a1_gen_endings/negation, not new.

SELF-VERIFICATION caught five real leaks before shipping, all via check_new.py, none of which the auditor would have caught on its own: (1) a draft use item paired Kup with chleba (genitive) on the assumption chleb takes the -u masculine default the course's own gen_endings rule states — chleba is NOT taught (chleb happens to be one of the many real-world exceptions to that simplified rule). Replaced with wodę/wody throughout, both regular -a→-y feminine forms already taught. (2) A draft used pisać/pisze as a fourth present-class model — pisze was never taught (only the infinitive pisać and the noun pisanie are in POOL, never a conjugated present form) — dropped; pić alone carries the present_e_esz slot, and mówić plus the perfective kup carry the bare-consonant case twice over from two different classes, so nothing is lost. (3) A first draft of the recap table derived Daj from dać→da, exactly the fifth chunk a2_imperative's own note says was deliberately left opaque — caught, removed from the table and from a quiz item, replaced with a second słuchaj recap question. (4) A draft slide-4 line used ale ('but') to join the two aspect-flip pairs — NEW, not taught anywhere — replaced with two plain sentences back to back. (5) Four quiz distractors (Grajesz!, Mówij!, Kupujej!, Pijej!) were fabricated non-words showing a plausible rule-misapplication rather than real Polish — replaced with real, already-taught, grammatically genuine forms in the wrong slot instead (Gram!, Mówisz!, Kupujesz!, Pijesz!), matching the 'distractors should be real/pool-legal, not invented' convention already set by b1_conditional_sg/b1_conditional_pl. (6) A quiz item originally asked 'Which verb is deliberately NOT covered by this unit's rule?', naming robić/rób in the choices and answer — caught against the Kontrola stage contract ('real forms, not meta-questions about the language') and against this pack's own robić fence, which the note already promised would keep it unmentioned outside the note itself; replaced with a real-usage discrimination item, and the one remaining mention of robić/rób in the intro body prose was cut too, so the fence now holds exactly as claimed — the two words appear nowhere in learner-facing content, only in this note.

intro.title: Czekaj! Słuchaj! Idź! Chodź! Daj! — never actually random
intro.body:
Back in A2 you learned five words whole, with no rule behind them — just five things to memorise. Here is the rule most of them were quietly following the whole time.

Take the on/ona (3sg) present form of a verb. Drop its ending. If what is left ends in a vowel, add -j. If it already ends in a consonant — including a stem that already ends in j — you are done, say it as it stands.

Watch czekaj, słuchaj, idź and chodź fall straight out of that one move. (Daj stays exactly as opaque as it always was — its own dictionary form was never shown to you, and this unit doesn't change that.)
intro.body_pl: Czekać → czeka → Czekaj! Słuchać → słucha → Słuchaj!

rows: same rule, plus the dzie→dź sound you already know by heart
same rule, plus the dzi→dź sound you already know by heart

intro.title: New verbs, the same rule
intro.body:
Three more present-tense classes, three more imperatives, no new mechanism.

grać → gra — ends in a vowel, so it takes -j, exactly like czekaj: Graj!
mówić → mówi — drop the -i and what is left, mów, already ends in a consonant. Nothing is added: Mów!
kupować → kupuje — drop the -e and the stem underneath, kupuj, already ends in j. Nothing more to add: Kupuj!
pić → pije — same story: drop -e, pij is already there, already ends in j: Pij!

Two different endings on the paper (vowel-final vs consonant-final), one instruction: add -j only if you need to.
intro.body_pl: Grać → gra → Graj! Mówić → mówi → Mów! Kupować → kupuje → Kupuj! Pić → pije → Pij!

rows: ends in consonant w → bare, nothing added
stem already ends in j → bare
stem already ends in j → bare

intro.title: One more source: the future
intro.body:
Perfective verbs have no present tense at all — the form that looks like a present (kupię, kupisz, kupi) is actually their future, the one you met in b1_perf_future. The imperative rule does not care where the 3sg form comes from. It works exactly the same way on it.

kupić → kupi (its future 3sg) → drop the -i → kup, already a bare consonant stem: Kup!
wypić → wypije (its future 3sg) → drop the -e → wypij, already ends in j: Wypij!

This rule works cleanly on every verb in this unit. A few common verbs need one extra sound change on top of it — those are for a later unit, not this one.
intro.body_pl: Kupić → kupi → Kup! Wypić → wypije → Wypij!

rows: bare consonant stem, from the future
stem already ends in j, from the future

intro.title: Saying don't — always the soft version
intro.body:
One rule, stated once: a negative command always takes the IMPERFECTIVE verb — even when the positive command you'd use is perfective.

Kup wodę! is fine for one bottle, bought and done. But Nie kup wody! is not something a Pole says. The negative has to be Nie kupuj wody! — kupować, not kupić — because nie turns the action into an ongoing prohibition, not a single finished event, and only the imperfective can carry that meaning.

Same story with drinking: Wypij herbatę! (drink it up, once) but Nie pij herbaty! (don't drink [any/it], generally) — never Nie wypij.

Nothing new is being built here: kupować, pić, and the genitive after nie (wody, herbaty) are all things you already had. The only new fact is the flip itself — say it, don't derive it.
intro.body_pl: Kup wodę! Nie kupuj wody! Wypij herbatę! Nie pij herbaty!

quiz.explain: gra already ends in the vowel a, so the rule adds -j: Graj!
Drop the -i and mów already ends in a consonant — nothing more to add.
Drop the -e; the stem kupuj already ends in j, so nothing is added on top.
Same move as kupuje→kupuj: drop -e, the j is already there.

quiz.prompt: Your son is about to buy one bottle of water and be done — a single errand. You say:
quiz.explain: One bottle, finished — the perfective imperative from kupić's future stem kupi.

quiz.prompt: You want your son to STOP buying bottled water in general, from now on. You say:
quiz.explain: A general prohibition is always imperfective — nie kup wody is not something a Pole says, even though positive Kup wodę! is fine.

quiz.prompt: Your granddaughter is about to finish her tea in one go before you leave. You say:
quiz.explain: Drink it up, once, done — the perfective wypić, not the ongoing pić.

quiz.prompt: You think your granddaughter shouldn't drink tea in the evening at all. You say:
quiz.explain: The negative always takes pić, the imperfective — nie wypij does not exist as a Polish command.

quiz.prompt: Your grandson is playing loudly right next to the baby, who is asleep. You say:
quiz.explain: Nie graj! stops the noisy action itself. Nie mów! and Nie pij! tell him to stop completely different things.
The word you already knew from A2, now derived: słucha ends in a vowel, so the rule adds -j, exactly like czeka→czekaj.
